health-tech-dd78ec0715.headline: Pharma supply chains are becoming more dependent on China and India
health-tech-dd78ec0715.fulltext:
- Europe and the US rely heavily on China and India for APIs and key starting materials, but shifting sourcing from China to India does not necessarily remove the risk because India itself depends heavily on Chinese inputs.
- Geopolitical tensions, tariffs and supply disruptions are forcing companies and governments to prioritise resilience, alternative sources and strategic buffers. The focus is increasingly on securing critical dependencies across the entire value chain, not just finished medicines.
- China and India are expanding their capabilities in finished pharmaceutical products, raising the prospect that Europe’s current upstream reliance on APIs could evolve into dependence on finished medicines. Building resilience will therefore require closer industry-government cooperation, multi-tier supply-chain visibility and deliberate redundancy rather than simply finding the lowest-cost supplier.
Pharmaceutical supply chains are becoming increasingly exposed to China and India, not only for active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and key starting materials, but potentially for finished medicines as well.
The industry is moving away from a model built primarily around cost efficiency towards one in which strategic optionality, political risk and supply security are becoming increasingly important. The shift is particularly significant for Europe and the US, both of which remain major pharmaceutical manufacturing and trading centres while relying heavily on external sources for critical upstream inputs.
The upstream dependency problem
The biggest exposure sits upstream in the pharmaceutical value chain. Europe obtains around 67 percent of the APIs used in its pharmaceutical production from outside the region, while the US relies on external sources for an even larger proportion.
Europe is also heavily dependent on external suppliers for key starting materials. China has become particularly important, with India representing another significant source.
The apparent diversification can nevertheless be misleading. India itself relies heavily on China for pharmaceutical inputs, meaning that switching procurement from China to India does not necessarily eliminate the underlying Chinese dependency.
This creates a more complex resilience challenge than simply adding another country to a supplier list.
“The pharmaceutical industry is very much dependent on China and India when we look at APIs and key starting materials,”
Dr Vincent Van Bockstaele, University of Antwerp explained, speaking on Day One of the 2026 Pharma.Aero Masterclass at the Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences. “And if you look at India, India itself is very dependent on China, so if you move from China to India, you have not necessarily solved the dependency problem.”
From cost efficiency to strategic optionality
The changing geopolitical environment is forcing pharmaceutical companies and policymakers to reconsider the traditional focus on lowest-cost sourcing.
Germany remains the world’s largest pharmaceutical exporter by value, while Belgium is also among the leading exporters. Frankfurt and Brussels have consequently developed major roles in global pharmaceutical airfreight.
But the strength of the downstream European pharmaceutical industry can obscure the vulnerability of its upstream supply base.
The strategic question is therefore no longer simply where medicines can be manufactured most efficiently. It is where the industry can maintain sufficient alternatives if geopolitical conditions interrupt existing flows.
“The question is no longer where can we source the cheapest or where can we manufacture the cheapest,” Van Bockstaele explained. “Due to the increasing focus on resilience, we are moving from cost efficiency towards strategic optionality.”
Two different policy responses
The US and Europe are responding differently to the growing strategic importance of pharmaceutical supply chains.
The US has increasingly framed medicines and pharmaceutical production through a national-security lens, with tariffs and incentives intended to encourage domestic or regional manufacturing.
Europe has placed greater emphasis on resilience by design, including regulatory measures, strategic investment and efforts to reinforce pharmaceutical production and critical supply chains.
Neither approach completely removes dependency. The pharmaceutical industry remains globally interconnected, and rebuilding every stage of production domestically would be costly and potentially inefficient.
The policy challenge is therefore to identify which dependencies are genuinely strategic and where intervention can make the greatest difference.
“Everything starts with patient access,” Van Bockstaele stated. “Policymakers are now looking not only at finished production, but increasingly at the critical ingredients and components coming from China and India, because those dependencies can directly affect the availability of medicines.”
The tariff effect
Trade policy is already changing pharmaceutical supply-chain behaviour. The major inventory pull-forward into the US around the tariff uncertainty of 2025, when pharmaceutical companies increased shipments was designed to build buffers before potential trade restrictions took effect.
The episode demonstrated how quickly policy uncertainty can translate into physical logistics activity. But the impact looked different depending on whether it was measured by trade value or physical volume.
Because pharmaceutical products are extremely high value relative to their weight, a relatively modest movement in physical quantities can produce a much larger change in the value of trade.
That distinction is important for airfreight, where high-value pharmaceuticals can make trade-value statistics appear considerably more volatile than underlying physical flows.
“There was a huge inventory pull-forward, with a lot more pharmaceutical products transported to make sure that, whatever happened with the tariffs, there would be some buffers or safety stock,” Van Bockstaele outlined. “But when we look at physical products, we did not see the same effect: the decline was much smaller than the decline in trade value.”
Airfreight stays stable as ocean grows
Despite the growing strategic importance of air cargo for pharmaceuticals, data shows that the long-term picture is more nuanced.
Europe-US pharmaceutical airfreight has remained relatively stable over roughly the past decade, while maritime transport has absorbed much of the growth in overall trade.
That does not diminish airfreight’s role. Pharmaceuticals remain particularly suited to air transport where products are high value, temperature sensitive or time critical, and geopolitical disruption can make speed an important form of resilience.
China-US pharmaceutical trade has also experienced significant changes around tariff developments, although airfreight has remained comparatively stable.
The data suggests that airfreight is therefore not simply following every movement in total pharmaceutical trade. Its role is shaped by the characteristics and value of the products being moved, as well as by the strategic requirements of the supply chain.
“Europe and the US are still very strong in pharmaceutical production further downstream,” Van Bockstaele laid out. “But when you look upstream, for APIs and key starting materials, we are much more dependent on China and India.”
China moves downstream
China and India are already among the largest and fastest-growing pharmaceutical exporters when measured by physical weight, while Europe and the US remain dominant in higher-value pharmaceutical trade.
The existing upstream dependency could increasingly be followed by downstream dependency as China develops greater capabilities in finished pharmaceutical products.
That would represent a more profound strategic challenge for Europe, because dependence would no longer be concentrated in the ingredients needed to manufacture medicines. It could extend to the medicines themselves.
The trend is already visible in growing European imports of finished pharmaceutical products from China and India.
“If we already have a very strong upstream dependency on APIs and key starting materials from China and India, the question is whether this will also become a downstream dependency,” Van Bockstaele stated.
“Will China produce more high-value pharmaceutical products and will we become increasingly dependent on China for the products we use every day?”
Resilience needs industry and government
The data points towards a difficult conclusion: diversification alone will not necessarily create resilience.
Adding India as a second source may still leave a supply chain exposed if the Indian pharmaceutical industry depends on Chinese inputs. Similarly, bringing some production closer to European or US markets does not automatically resolve vulnerabilities elsewhere in the value chain.
Resilience therefore requires a broader redesign of pharmaceutical networks, with governments and companies considering critical dependencies across multiple tiers.
That means accepting some redundancy, identifying strategic products and inputs, maintaining alternative sources and recognising that the cheapest supply chain may not be the most secure one.
It also requires greater cooperation between policymakers and industry. Governments need a better understanding of how pharmaceutical supply chains actually operate, while companies need to incorporate geopolitical considerations into network decisions rather than treating them as an external risk.
“If every party continues pushing the next party towards the lowest sourcing cost, we will keep reproducing the same dependencies,” Van Bockstaele concluded. “We need more interaction between policymakers and industry, and they need to understand how pharmaceutical supply chains actually work.”

agritech-11ae32110a.headline: 33% of India’s land is degraded: Why the soil crisis threatens farming and food security
agritech-11ae32110a.fulltext:
33% of India’s land is degraded: Why the soil crisis threatens farming and food security
Regenerative farming can involve practices such as reduced tillage, cover cropping, crop rotation, agroforestry and livestock integration
- Sep 16, 2026,
- Updated Sep 16, 2026 2:05 AM IST
Nearly one-third of India’s soil is already degraded, raising concerns over agricultural productivity, farmer livelihoods and the country’s long-term food security, according to the report Reimagining Indian Agriculture: Unlocking the Regenerative Opportunity.
The report cites data from the Soil Physics Division of the ICAR-Indian Institute of Soil Science, which estimates that 115–120 million hectares, or around 33% of India’s total land area, had been degraded by 2024.
The scale of degradation matters because soil is the foundation of India’s farm economy. As soil quality declines, the ability of farmland to support stable and productive agriculture can weaken. The report links soil degradation with rising risks to agricultural productivity, farmer livelihoods and long-term food security. It also points to climate variability and groundwater depletion as additional pressures increasing production risks.
READ THIS: Avocado boom in India: how farmers are turning a premium fruit into a new income source
What is driving the concern?
The report argues that restoring degraded land requires a shift towards regenerative agriculture, an approach that seeks not merely to maintain farmland but to rebuild soil health, biodiversity, water resources and ecosystem functions.
Regenerative farming can involve practices such as reduced tillage, cover cropping, crop rotation, agroforestry and livestock integration. These methods are designed to increase soil organic matter, improve nutrient and water cycles and reduce dependence on synthetic inputs.
The challenge, however, is taking these practices to scale. The report identifies high transition costs, limited access to finance, underdeveloped carbon and ecosystem markets, weak monitoring systems and uncertainty over short-term farm productivity as major barriers.
ALSO READ: 90 million litres of glacier water every day: How Ladakh is reviving 1,000 acres of farmland
India already has programmes, but a policy gap remains
India has several initiatives aligned with regenerative farming. The National Mission on Natural Farming has received ₹2,481 crore and targets one crore farmers for training and adoption. The AgriSURE Fund has a corpus of ₹750 crore, while the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana provides ₹31,500 per hectare for three years for organic clusters.
Yet, the report says India lacks a nationally accepted definition and unified framework for regenerative agriculture. It recommends shifting government support from input-based subsidies towards incentives linked to measurable outcomes such as soil organic carbon, water productivity, lower input intensity, biodiversity and farmer income stability.

india-deep-tech-22ba858b84.fulltext:
Insider Brief
- Robocurve raised $10 million in seed funding to expand its independent testing of how well frontier AI models control real robots and to support open robotics benchmarks.
- Initialized Capital led the round, with participation from Notable Capital, Decasonic, Y Combinator, Halcyon Futures and others, while Robocurve plans to expand its research team, robot testing and academic benchmarking programs.
- The company said large language models are improving quickly on robotics tasks, citing tests where they outperformed some specialized VLA models and output-token speeds rising about 2.1 times per month, though latency and generalization to more complex robots remain open questions.
Robocurve has raised $10 million in seed funding to expand its work evaluating how well frontier artificial intelligence models control real robots. As a Public Benefit Corporation, Robocurve indicated it operates as a third-party auditor and develops open-source tools and benchmarks designed to measure what AI models can do when connected to physical machines.
Initialized Capital led the round, with participation from Notable Capital, Decasonic, Y Combinator, Halcyon Futures and other investors. The company plans to use the funding to grow its research team, test a wider range of robots and tasks and support academic researchers developing open robotics benchmarks.
Robocurve said its evaluations are designed to remain independent from the AI companies whose models it tests. The company sets its own research agenda and methodology and publishes results without giving frontier AI labs control over the findings.
“The widespread deployment of general-purpose robots could have profound implications for the social contract and the labor market, and deserves a whole-of-society approach to help families prepare for the changes ahead, even if the precise timing of the arrival of such technology still has large uncertainties,” the company noted in a blog post announcing the funding. “When the clouds are heavy, we don’t need to know exactly when it will rain to carry an umbrella.”
AI Models Controlling Robots
As general-purpose AI models increasingly show an ability to perform robotics tasks that previously required models built specifically for robotics, Robocurve said its research has found that large language models can outperform some vision-language-action, or VLA, models on simple robotic tasks.
The company said more recent frontier models have also completed tasks that earlier systems struggled with, though Robocurve noted that major technical questions remain. Among them are whether those capabilities will extend to robots with more complex bodies, such as dexterous hands and humanoids, and whether inference speeds can become fast enough for real-time control.
Robocurve pointed out that latency remains one of the main limits on using large language models to control robots directly.
Robocurve said frontier language models are also improving quickly at controlling robots. The company pointed to tests in which large language models outperformed specialized vision-language-action models on simple tasks and said some tasks that models struggled with a month earlier could be completed easily by newer systems. Robocurve also cited a roughly 2.1-times monthly increase in output-token speed for frontier models, arguing that faster inference could make real-time robot control practical sometime between late 2026 and 2029 if the trend continues.
Robocurve
The company was incorporated about three months ago and said its research has since received more than 6 million views. Its Inspect Robots open-source evaluation framework has been downloaded more than 97,000 times, according to the company.
The company operates a benchmarking program that provides academic groups with funding and robot hardware to develop open-source evaluations. Robocurve said it is making a total of $500,000 available through the program and providing YAM robotic arms to participating research teams.
Robocurve also said researchers from more than 200 institutions have signed up to build benchmarks through its academic program, including participants from 19 of the world’s 20 highest-ranked universities.

global-economics-b251803cde.headline: Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risks
global-economics-b251803cde.fulltext: Experts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis. Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExperts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis. Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesExplainerCould AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksWe examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI developmentThere have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop.Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them.‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University.It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”.With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said.Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said.Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still.Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system.One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios.“These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.“If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work.Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet.Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”.'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime?The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”.Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals.View image in fullscreenElon Musk, CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have said AI firms should slow down AI development. Composite: Fabrice Coffrini; Julien de Rosa; Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said.“If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said. 'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026“Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.”But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035.The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems.AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making.'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology.The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”.Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going.“The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.”'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown.This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications.Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”.Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models.These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicEthicsSam AltmanElon MuskOpenAIDatacentresexplainersShareReuse this content

india-e55fb7ae65.headline: U.S. House advances Russia sanctions Bill that seeks 100% tariffs on India, others; set for final vote
india-e55fb7ae65.fulltext:
The U.S. House of Representatives voted to advance a Bill that would authorise President Donald Trump to impose 100% tariffs on India and other countries for buying oil and gas from Russia and extend existing sanctions on Iran.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening (September 15, 2026) after two Democratic lawmakers broke ranks with the party and voted in favour with the Republicans.
The resolution to advance the Russia sanctions Bill and a slew of other legislations was approved by a 214-211 vote, shocking the House Democratic leadership. The Bill is expected to come up for a final vote in the House on Wednesday (September 16, 2026).
Democratic Congressman Gregory Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, on Monday (September 24, 2026) opposed the Russia sanctions bill contending that it would grant President Trump unchecked authority to impose tariffs without any guardrails.
Last month, the U.S. Senate passed the Bill with an overwhelming 86-11 majority. The Bill seeks to impose sanctions not only on Russia’s leadership and energy sector, but also on the "shadow fleet" of vessels that enable Moscow to evade sanctions on oil deliveries.
The vote on the Bill is taking place at a time when pro-Ukraine groups have stepped up efforts to lobby support for their cause.
The Ukraine Action Summit, organised by the American Coalition for Ukraine, is underway here to lobby with US lawmakers for continued support of Kyiv.
The U.S. believes that Russia’s crude oil trade is funding the war against Ukraine. The Bill also seeks to authorise President Donald Trump to impose 100% tariffs on Russia’s top oil trading partners including China and India.
The Bill passed by the U.S. Senate on August 7 does not name Russia’s trading partners, but mentions five largest importers of oil and gas by volume.
The Bill has to be passed by the House of Representatives before it is sent to the President for signature. The House breaks into early recess on Thursday (September 17, 2026) and is expected to reconvene on November 9 after the midterm elections.

india-bcc517d3b0.headline: Tanker El Gaia hit in the Strait of Hormuz was operating in ‘dark mode’
india-bcc517d3b0.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-bcc517d3b0.fulltext:
MT El Gaia, the tanker which was hit by a projectile over the weekend in the Strait of Hormuz, was reportedly operating in “dark mode,” with its Automatic Identification System (AIS) switched off, and its coordinates were not available at the time of reporting. Its last port of call was Sohar, Oman.
The tanker had 25 crew members on board: 14 Indian and 11 Pakistani nationals.
Two crew members remain unaccounted for: Muhammad Hammad Obaida, Third Engineer, a Pakistani national from Karachi who had joined the vessel on September 7, 2026; and Sumit Kumar Singh, Oiler, an Indian national from Vaishali who had joined on June 25, 2026.
Photos of the ship from September 13 indicate that the engine room was attacked and damaged by the projectile. The two were reportedly on watch in the engine room at the time of the incident.
Sumit Kumar Singh had signed on to the ship in June when the ship had called on Dahej, Gujarat.
The 20-year-old ship, which has a cargo-carrying capacity of 48,000 tonnes, is owned and managed by Dubai, UAE-based companies. Five recruitment agencies supplied the crew onboard the vessel, according to official sources.
The Omani Coast Guard boarded the vessel following the attack. The remaining 23 crew members were transferred to an Omani Coast Guard vessel and brought ashore. While the Master and Chief Engineer were Pakistani nationals, the Chief Officer, Second Engineer and others were Indians.
The Indian Government has not attributed any responsibility for the attack. Iran’s IRGC Navy has said the tanker struck naval mines while using what it calls an illegal route south of the strait. The United States has disputed this, saying the vessel was struck by a missile and later a drone.

world-7e51f55f4e.headline: Nato jets down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace
world-7e51f55f4e.fulltext:
Nato jets down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace
- Published
Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.
It is thought to be the first time that a Nato jet has shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace.
Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.
Shortly after midnight local time (21:00 GMT), alerts were sent to phones in the region, warning of a potential drone incursion and telling residents to "find a safe place" and "wait for the all clear".
Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.
Nausėda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Moscow has not commented on the incident.
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
The drone debris, scattered widely, will be collected and examined to try to determine who it belonged to, whether it was armed - and whether it was launched at Lithuania deliberately or perhaps strayed off course.
Lithuania, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.
Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.
Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions", it added.
Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.
Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

Central Command confirms engagement off Iranian coast as Tehran claims vessels were local fishing craft
The US military said on Tuesday that it opened fire and destroyed two small Iranian boats this week that were trying to steal a drone ship in the waters off Iran, the latest back-and-forth fire in the stalemated war.
Captain Tim Hawkins, US Central Command spokesman, said the Iranian boats “recently attempted to take possession of a US unmanned surface vessel” but failed after the military “forcefully responded”.
Iranian state media reported on Monday that a pair of fishing boats came under attack in Hormozgan province on Iran’s southern coast and that several fishermen were reported missing, citing a provincial official.

other-interests-598f0f586c.headline: ‘They should choose their own destinies’: Manish Chandi on India’s isolated tribes
other-interests-598f0f586c.fulltext:
- Mongabay interviewed Manish Chandi, a former research scholar who has spent over two decades working on tribal communities, about the latest threats and activities affecting the lives of isolated and contacted tribal peoples living in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands off the southeastern coast of mainland India.
- Isolated tribes, which maintain little to no contact with outsiders, face threats ranging from trawlers entering buffer waters and development projects planned in hunting grounds, to government perspectives that can limit their independence and capacity to decide their future on their own terms.
- Chandi discusses the impact of curious outsiders trying to visit isolated tribes, how contact can affect different tribes differently and how to protect isolated peoples’ autonomy.
- Tribal reserves are large biodiversity hotspots, rivaling protected areas and wildlife sanctuaries in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, says Chandi.
From above, the North Sentinel Island tribal reserve in India’s Andaman and Nicobar archipelago is a thick, unbroken patch of dark green — starkly surrounded by the shimmering coastal blue waters of its buffer zone.
On these shores, Sentinelese people, who live in voluntary isolation protected by a strict government no-contact policy, spear fish, hunt turtles and collect mollusks in shallow reefs surrounded by mangroves. The coastal reefs are intact ecosystems rich in fish life, say biologists.
“I have seen them [groups of men, women and children] foraging and collecting these food resources during low tide on several occasions,” says Manish Chandi, a tribal expert who has watched the island from afar. “The Sentinelese are aware of these as nutritious and sparsely available resources in such [mangrove] habitats, which are very few on and around the island.”
Like other tribal reserves on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, in the southeast of mainland India, North Sentinel Island is a biodiversity hotspot; and, like other tribal reserves, the isolated people who live there have attracted influencers and misunderstandings, says Chandi.
“Curiosity and ignorance regarding the islanders is quite high and understandably so amongst outsiders and [government] bureaucrats who have little association with the islands,” he tells Mongabay in an interview.
There are six recognized tribes living in the reserves and islands of the archipelago — some tribes have experienced full contact while others, such as Sentinelese and Shompen people, live in voluntary isolation. The Shompen in the Great Nicobar tribal reserve maintain minimal contact with officials but prevent outsiders from entering their reserve forests and remain clear on “non-interference and wanting interactions on their terms.”
In the Andaman Islands, the Ang people (also known as ‘Jarawa’) in the Jarawa tribal reserve maintain limited contact, while the Onge in their tribal reserve are settled and have ongoing interactions with the Andaman administration. The Great Andamanese, whose population greatly declined due to disease and colonization, are fully contacted as are the Nicobarese of the Nicobar archipelago who are integrated into mainstream Indian society.
The isolated tribes, including those with limited contact, are facing potential threats, many of which are outside their control, says Chandi.
Near North Sentinel Island, fishers and trawlers are encroaching inside buffer waters and exploiting sharks, crabs and marine resources that Sentinelese people depend on, he says. In Great Nicobar Island, he adds, a planned large-scale development project overlaps with foraging and hunting lands of the Shompen people.
According to Chandi, many of the issues tribes face are grounded in social and governmental misunderstanding, through which relatively isolated peoples are viewed as primitive and in need of industrial development and which deny their need to access their land and food resources to maintain self-sufficiency and a capability to decide their future on their own terms.
“Some officials in the islands do not see this as a priority and … consider supplies of external food resources as a means to well-being,” he says. “This has actually caused the increased dependence on supplies of food that the communities cannot grow or gather themselves and eventually makes them immensely dependent on governmental mechanisms.”
“Resource exploitation by non-tribals makes dependence on governmental schemes of rehabilitation the only possibility: It makes once independent communities who were geographically spread across their own landscapes and territories, sedentary and ensconced within reservations using accommodation built for them, leaving the larger landscape devoid of their presence and use … This has more recently resulted in denotification attempts [state-led removal of a legally protected status], developmental visions and proposals to transform some lands of tribal reserves into tourism or business enclaves.”
To further understand the latest threats and activities affecting the lives of tribal peoples living in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Mongabay interviewed Chandi, a former research scholar who has spent two and a half decades working on tribal communities with the Andaman Nicobar Environment Team and Nature Conservation Foundation. He was an advisory board member of the Tribal Research Institute, part of the Andaman and Nicobar Administration’s Department of Tribal Welfare, from 2011-2019. Chandi is currently a consultant in social ecology.
This interview was edited for length and clarity.
Mongabay: You’ve said that tribal reserves in India’s Andaman and Nicobar Islands, such as the North Sentinel Island and the Great Nicobar Island tribal reserves which are home to voluntarily isolated Sentinelese and Shompen people, are among the best biodiversity hotspots as well as culturally unique spaces. Why is that? And what has enabled them to maintain such richness?
Manish Chandi: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands have approximately 100-odd declared protected areas, that include wildlife sanctuaries, national parks (marine and terrestrial) and a biosphere reserve as well. Among all these, none of them compare in size, biodiversity, both density and diversity, of flora and fauna on both the island land and nearshore or coral reef habitats to what exists in the tribal reserves of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
This is primarily because the areas declared as tribal reserves are large and encompass geographical extents of where each tribal community exists. In the case of the Onge tribal reserve on Little Andaman Island, for example, the geography encompasses everywhere the Onge existed during their declaration in 1950. All these tribal reserved areas have not been used for timber extraction and settlement and therefore retain the biodiversity of both various habitats and also species — both endemic and otherwise.
Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve is the only area that has a biosphere reserve that includes a tribal reserve too [home to the Shompen people who live in voluntary isolation], and is the single largest area in the Nicobar archipelago. Meanwhile, the Jarawa tribal reserve [home to the Ang, as the community call themselves, who are not in voluntary isolation] is the single largest tribal reserve in the Andaman, even in comparison to the Nicobar islands.
The Jarawa reserve and the Onge reserve are the largest and most important biodiversity repository in the Andaman Islands, which is composed of a range of habitat and species.
The tribal reserves have remained relatively intact, except that with cultural change and acculturation [the adoption of the cultural traits and values of others], poachers and infiltrators from within the Andaman Islands have begun exploiting the tribal reserves for biological resources including lobsters and crabs, fish, timber, wild pigs, deer and birds from the Onge and Jarawa tribal reserves in particular.
It is because of their declaration as tribal reserves and, more importantly, the original hostility of the inhabitants, that poachers took a while to reach and begin exploitation. But they have done some luring and made friends with some inhabitants. Poor enforcement of the Wildlife (Protection Act), 1972; the Forest (Conservation Act), 1980; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation; and the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, adds to the problem.
Mongabay: Species of mangrove and littoral mangrove species surround the areas of North Sentinel Island where the uncontacted Sentinelese people live. Biologists are unable to conduct studies there, but do you know what species these are exactly? Are these reef patches important to the Sentinelese people? And do these species of mangrove face any threats?
Manish Chandi: The island of North Sentinel is devoid of any major saltwater inlets or creeks, there are just a few minor ones. Mangroves are sparsely scattered in patches of the island’s coast. The southeastern shore has a small emergent reef which is like an islet, on which littoral mangrove vegetation has colonized and established (I forget the specific species, but they are not the more common varieties of Rhizophora or Bruguiera).
The species I recall are more littoral and those that survive in rocky saltwater habitats rather than mangrove marsh, which is specifically absent on the island.
These shallow-water patches and habitat are a very important resource of edible bivalves and mollusks for the Sentinelese islanders. I have seen them, groups of men, women and children, foraging and collecting these food resources during low tide on several occasions. The Sentinelese are aware of these as nutritious and sparsely available resources in a type of habitat that is very scarce on and around the island.
Beyond these patches, there are several major coral reefs all around the island. These vary in size, placement and distribution. They include shallows, deep-water reefs and shelves also. These habitats are among the most important food resource for the Sentinelese, as they are rich in fish life. The Sentinelese punt their canoes over these nearshore habitats, as far as their punting poles can still reach the bottom, to hunt fish and turtle.
Fishermen from the Andamans also encroach upon these habitats — not just in South Andaman, but nowadays, even those from far away such as Middle Andaman — for sharks and export-value fish, crabs and lobsters. South Andaman fishers have long evaded detection when using these waters as there has been no real patrolling by administrative machinery, except for stray instances when an official would tour the region around North Sentinel, reprimand any fishermen or poachers in the vicinity and let them off.
This laxity has emboldened these same resource exploiters to venture further in and closer to the shores to reach the salable marine resources that the Sentinelese depend on and exploit them for their own gain. They bring these to the export markets and sell at fish landing centres in South Andaman, particularly at Wandoor and Guptapara villages.
Sea turtles, such as green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas) and hawksbill sea turtles (Eretmochelys imbricata), are found locally in these waters and are exploited by poachers and fishermen who both spear and lay nets in nearshore waters. The Sentinelese, on the other hand, use bow and arrows or harpoons to hunt fish and turtles in their waters for survival.
This unequal use and exploitation between non-tribal peoples from the Andaman and the Sentinelese Islanders is very concerning, particularly with the poor implementation of laws and regulations regarding the future of the Indigenous islanders.

other-interests-b1ba40027b.headline: Roads, infrastructure prevent tigers from settling in Indian tiger reserve
other-interests-b1ba40027b.fulltext:
A forested tiger reserve in southern India is home to a thriving population of spotted and sambar deer, nilgai antelopes, and wild pigs — all ideal prey for tigers. Yet the reserve has no resident tigers, reports contributor Nivedhika Krishnan for Mongabay India.
Kawal Tiger Reserve in the state of Telangana connects key tiger populations in the reserves of Tadoba-Andhari, in Maharashtra state to the west, and Indravati, in Chhattisgarh state to the east. Since 2015, researchers have confirmed that only 15 tigers entered Kawal from Maharashtra. Of these, only two were females.
Lead researcher Imran Siddiqui told Mongabay India that tigers traveling from Maharashtra to Kawal face heavy infrastructure throughout their journey.
“The corridor is fragmented by open-cast coal mines, the Ada irrigation project, electrified farm fences, and the main Hyderabad-Nagpur railway line,” Siddiqui said. “National Highway 44 acts as the most formidable barrier of all with its heavy traffic and high fencing. It isn’t just one obstacle — it is a cumulative mosaic of risks that forces dispersing tigers to turn back.”
He added that while male tigers dispersing from their birthplace are “bolder risk-takers” and can move long distances through human-dominated landscapes, female tigers are more risk-averse and “require quiet, undisturbed habitat to raise cubs.”
“Crossing busy highways, railways, and mines poses a massive perceived threat to females,” Siddiqui said. “That is why males occasionally dodge traffic to reach Kawal, but females turn back. Without females, you simply cannot build a breeding population.”
Anish Andheria, president and CEO of the Wildlife Conservation Trust, told Mongabay India that the reserve itself needs a core area free from human settlements, like in India’s other tiger reserves. As of 2023, there were 37 villages and 67 small settlements inside Kawal Tiger Reserve’s core, he said.
But keeping people out of the ecosystem is a fraught issue. When Kawal was declared a tiger reserve in 2012, authorities had promised the resident Indigenous communities, the Adivasis, that the change wouldn’t harm their legal rights or survival, said Siddam Bhujang Rao, a local Adivasi leader. “But once the reserve was established, their stance completely shifted.”
Families who were relocated from the core reserve, for instance, received little of what was promised to them in the official relocation package for the villages, Rao said.
“They promised us land, water, and model villages,” he said. “Instead, families were moved to houses with crumbling plaster, and the agricultural lands were never handed over.”
Wildlife managers have also floated the idea of “assisted dispersal,” where wild female tigers from dense populations in states like Maharashtra are airlifted directly into Kawal. But Siddiqui warned that such manual translocations aren’t “a shortcut for fixing broken corridors.”
“Bringing tigers from outside will not work,” Rao agreed. “It is a flawed idea, and it should be abandoned.”

beyond-your-beat-9b1c20e232.headline: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google have been in talks on AI safety for weeks
beyond-your-beat-9b1c20e232.fulltext:
Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s global policy chief, told reporters on Tuesday that the company has been working with rivals Anthropic and Google DeepMind on AI safety for weeks, as first reported by Bloomberg. Lehane is reportedly in Washington to work with U.S. lawmakers addressing catastrophic risks associated with AI.
The revelation comes in the wake of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay, published Saturday, which called for the industry to work together to slow the pace of frontier AI and avoid catastrophic risks. AI leaders across the industry, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google’s Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, supported Amodei’s letter and call to action, with Altman saying that OpenAI would join Anthropic in embedding third-party evaluators into the company to monitor for safety.
On Tuesday, Lehane admitted that the three companies have been in talks for several weeks regarding AI safety. Some, including Altman, have noted that such talks could put the companies at risk of violating antitrust law if the coordination is found to suppress competition. Amodei’s essay proposed a narrow government waiver allowing such safety coordination, but Lehane reportedly said the firms don’t need one.
The news confirms earlier reporting and hints that the companies were working together. In an interview with Fortune late last week, Altman hinted that he had been in private discussions with other AI leaders. This week, The Information reported that the three companies have been working together to create a standards body for the AI industry — something Altman reportedly told staff would need to happen without the support of the U.S. government.
Hassabis called on the U.S. in July to establish a new standards body to act as an AI watchdog, with the power to screen the world’s most advanced models and coordinate industrywide slowdowns if dangers progressed.
President Trump, for his part, has dismissed safety concerns as a hoax and pushed back on the need for tighter regulations, saying any slowdown would give China a leg up in the race. His key AI advisor David Sacks — a longtime investor with a personal stake in much of the industry — echoed this, saying fears of existential risk from AI were overblown.
At the same Tuesday meeting, Lehane said that OpenAI supports a provision in the FRONTIER Act that would force top frontier labs to allow “independent verification organizations” into their companies to ensure models are developed safely.
TechCrunch has reached out to Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI for comment.

The part-time fellowship is remote within the United States, requires access to a major U.S. airport for travel, and involves 15–25 hours of work per week. About Partners for Public Good
Partners for Public Good is a nonpartisan organisation that works alongside state and local governments to strengthen the operational systems that determine whether public policy delivers results for residents.
Its work covers areas including public procurement, staffing, budgeting and technology. Rather than only providing recommendations, PPG works directly with government teams during implementation to help ensure that meaningful improvements are achieved.
Through applied research and its Procurement Excellence Network, which brings together more than 3,000 government professionals, PPG translates lessons from individual governments into knowledge and practical tools that can be used across jurisdictions.
About the Research Fellowship
The six-month fellowship is designed for researchers who want to apply rigorous research methods to real-world government challenges. Fellows will conduct policy-relevant research, collect and analyse data, and contribute to publications and other public-facing outputs.
Participants will work on a defined research project under the guidance of PPG staff and alongside two other fellows. The programme combines independent research with coaching calls, research team meetings, professional development and mentorship.
Each fellow will also participate in an in-person research retreat.
The fellowship is open to graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career faculty, research and policy professionals, and other candidates with comparable experience.
Research Topics
Fellows can choose from five priority research areas.
Understanding Public Procurement Through Municipal Data will examine publicly available information on local government procurement across U.S. cities and explore how governments purchase goods and services.
The Compliance Web: Layered Governance and Local Implementation will investigate how federal, state and local laws, regulations and funding requirements influence government implementation and administrative capacity.
Emerging Technology and Government Operations will explore how artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are being used by state and local governments and what these technologies reveal about government operations and organisational capacity.
Innovative Approaches to Public Purchasing will examine emerging procurement practices, particularly cooperative purchasing, and assess their implications for efficiency, market participation and the public procurement ecosystem.
Building Local Capacity for Stormwater Management will explore how communities develop and finance stormwater management capacity in response to infrastructure and climate resilience needs.
Fellowship Deliverables
Each fellow will be expected to complete approximately two to three deliverables during the programme. Depending on the selected research project, these may include a literature review, a dataset compiled from publicly available information, a dataset based on primary research, survey or interview instruments, a draft publication, policy brief or conference submission.
Fellows will receive support in translating their research into publications and policy-oriented outputs that can strengthen both the evidence base for government reform and their professional research portfolios.
Who Can Apply?
Applicants may be affiliated with a university, think tank, nonprofit organisation, research institution or policy organisation and may maintain that affiliation throughout the fellowship. Independent applicants without an institutional affiliation are also eligible to apply, provided they can meet the programme’s time and deliverable requirements.
The fellowship is particularly suited to candidates with research, policy analysis, data collection, qualitative or quantitative research, public administration, public policy or related experience.
Compensation and Benefits
Selected fellows will work 15–25 hours per week and receive US$50 per hour. Benefits will be provided where required by applicable state or local law.
The desired fellowship start date is October 2026, with the programme running for six months.
Eligibility and Work Authorisation
The fellowship is remote but is limited to candidates who are legally authorised to work in the United States. PPG explicitly states that it is unable to provide visa sponsorship.
Applicants should therefore confirm their current U.S. work authorisation before applying. The position also requires access to a major U.S. airport because fellows will be expected to travel for the in-person research retreat.
How to Apply
Applicants must submit the following materials by September 28, 2026:
- A resume or CV of no more than two pages.
- A letter of interest of no more than two pages addressing the applicant’s preferred research project, qualifications and proposed approach. Candidates interested in two projects may submit up to three pages and must identify their top choice.
- A work sample, which may be a published or under-review research paper or another product demonstrating relevant research skills and expertise.
PPG will review applications on a rolling basis, but applications received by close of business on September 28, 2026, will be considered.
